title: Synchronization — intrinsic monitors (object-level locks) prevent race conditions
shortTitle: How does synchronization work with intrinsic monitors?

s1_definition.profdef: Synchronization is Java's mechanism for controlling access to shared resources by multiple threads. Every Java object has an **intrinsic monitor lock** (also called monitor or mutex). When a thread enters a `synchronized` block/method, it ACQUIRES the monitor lock. Other threads trying to acquire the SAME lock are BLOCKED until the first thread releases it (exits the synchronized block). This guarantees **mutual exclusion** (only one thread in the critical section) and **visibility** (changes made by one thread are visible to the next thread that acquires the same lock). Without synchronization: race conditions — two threads read-modify-write the same variable simultaneously, producing corrupt results.
s1_definition.analogy: Every object in Java has an invisible PADLOCK. `synchronized(account)` = grab the padlock. Only ONE person can hold the padlock at a time. Other people trying to grab it WAIT in line (BLOCKED). When you release the padlock (exit synchronized), the next person in line grabs it. This prevents two tellers from simultaneously modifying Rajesh's balance — one waits while the other finishes. Without the padlock: Teller-1 reads balance Rs.100,000, Teller-2 reads Rs.100,000, both debit Rs.50,000, both write Rs.50,000. Expected Rs.0, got Rs.50,000. Rs.50,000 LOST.
s1_definition.oneliner: Every Java object has an intrinsic monitor lock. synchronized = acquire lock → mutual exclusion + visibility. Only ONE thread in critical section at a time. Others BLOCKED until lock released.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Synchronization is Java's mechanism for controlling access to shared resources by multiple threads. Every Java object has an **intrinsic monitor lock** (also called monitor or mutex). When a thread enters a `synchronized` block/method, it ACQUIRES the monitor lock. Other threads trying to acquire the SAME lock are BLOCKED until the first thread releases it (exits the synchronized block). This guarantees **mutual exclusion** (only one thread in the critical section) and **visibility** (changes made by one thread are visible to the next thread that acquires the same lock). Without synchronization: race conditions — two threads read-modify-write the same variable simultaneously, producing corrupt results.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Every object in Java has an invisible PADLOCK. `synchronized(account)` = grab the padlock. Only ONE person can hold the padlock at a time. Other people trying to grab it WAIT in line (BLOCKED). When you release the padlock (exit synchronized), the next person in line grabs it. This prevents two tellers from simultaneously modifying Rajesh's balance — one waits while the other finishes. Without the padlock: Teller-1 reads balance Rs.100,000, Teller-2 reads Rs.100,000, both debit Rs.50,000, both write Rs.50,000. Expected Rs.0, got Rs.50,000. Rs.50,000 LOST.

**One line to remember:** Every Java object has an intrinsic monitor lock. synchronized = acquire lock → mutual exclusion + visibility. Only ONE thread in critical section at a time. Others BLOCKED until lock released.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's real-time fund transfer service had a race condition.** Two simultaneous transfers from Rajesh's account (Rs.100,000 balance): Transfer-1 debits Rs.60,000, Transfer-2 debits Rs.50,000. Without synchronization: both read balance=100,000, both succeed, balance becomes Rs.50,000 or Rs.40,000 instead of rejecting one transfer (insufficient funds after the first). Fix: `synchronized` on the account object ensures only one transfer executes at a time. Transfer-1 debits → balance=40,000 → Transfer-2 checks → 40,000 < 50,000 → REJECTED. Correct behavior.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Rajesh's account has Rs.100,000. Two transfer threads start simultaneously.

**Step 2.** Thread-1 enters `synchronized void debit(60000)` → acquires monitor lock on the SafeAccount object. Thread-2 tries to enter `synchronized void debit(50000)` → lock held by Thread-1 → Thread-2 state = BLOCKED.

**Step 3.** Thread-1: checks balance(100000) >= 60000 → true → balance = 100000 - 60000 = 40000 → exits synchronized → lock released.

**Step 4.** Thread-2 acquires lock → checks balance(40000) >= 50000 → FALSE → debit rejected → exits synchronized.

**Step 5.** Final balance: Rs.40,000. Only one transfer succeeded. Without synchronization: both threads would read 100000, both succeed, balance would be either 50000 or 40000 (lost update).
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ RACE CONDITION (without sync) ═══

  Thread-1: read(100000) → compute(40000) → write(40000)
  Thread-2: read(100000) → compute(50000) →     write(50000)  ← OVERWRITES!
  Final: 50000 (or 40000). Rs.50,000 LOST!

  ═══ SYNCHRONIZED (with sync) ═══

  Thread-1: [LOCK] → read(100000) → write(40000) → [UNLOCK]
  Thread-2:  BLOCKED ──────────────────────────────→ [LOCK] → read(40000) → 40000<50000 → REJECT → [UNLOCK]
  Final: 40000. CORRECT! One transfer rejected.

  ═══ INTRINSIC MONITOR ═══
  Object header: [Mark Word | Class Pointer]
  Mark Word contains lock state:
  Unlocked → Biased → Lightweight (CAS) → Heavyweight (OS mutex)
  JVM escalates as contention increases.
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Java Object Monitor ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │     Java Object (any object)         │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────── │
  │  Object Header:                      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Mark Word (64 bits):            │ │
  │  │  - lock state (unlocked/biased/ │ │
  │  │    lightweight/heavyweight)     │ │
  │  │  - owning thread ID            │ │
  │  │  - hash code (when unlocked)   │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Monitor:                        │ │
  │  │  - owner: Thread (or null)      │ │
  │  │  - entrySet: [BLOCKED threads]  │ │
  │  │  - waitSet: [WAITING threads]   │ │
  │  │  - recursion count: int         │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  synchronized(obj):
  1. Check Mark Word lock state
  2. If unlocked → set owner = currentThread → enter
  3. If owned by currentThread → recursion++ (reentrant!)
  4. If owned by other → thread → entrySet (BLOCKED)
  5. Exit synchronized → owner = null → wake one from entrySet

  Lock escalation:
  No contention → Biased lock (zero overhead)
  Low contention → Lightweight lock (CAS spin)
  High contention → Heavyweight lock (OS mutex, thread parking)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Synchronization prevents race conditions by ensuring mutual exclusion — only one thread can execute a `synchronized` block on the same object at a time. Every Java object has an intrinsic monitor (built into the object header's Mark Word). When a thread enters `synchronized(obj)`, it acquires the monitor lock. Other threads trying to acquire the same lock are BLOCKED until it's released. The monitor also guarantees visibility: changes made inside the synchronized block are visible to the next thread that acquires the same lock (happens-before relationship).

The JVM optimizes monitor locks through lock escalation: biased locking (zero overhead when only one thread ever locks the object), lightweight locking (CAS-based for low contention), and heavyweight locking (OS mutex for high contention). The monitor has two sets: the entry set (BLOCKED threads waiting to acquire) and the wait set (WAITING threads that called wait()). In banking: fund transfer must be synchronized per account — two simultaneous debits on the same account without sync can cause lost updates (balance corruption). With sync: one transfer executes, the other checks the updated balance and may be rejected if insufficient.

---

keyPoints: Every Java object has an intrinsic lock (monitor)
synchronized acquires the monitor — one thread at a time
Other threads are BLOCKED until monitor released
Released on: method exit, block exit, or exception
